title: British film since 1995 (two-film study): Trainspotting and Shaun of the Dead

items.definition: Heroin addicts in 1980s Edinburgh reject “Choose Life” consumerism, but the ending endorses selfish individualism.
items.examples: Renton opens rejecting “a job, a career, a family, a big television” and ends promising to be “just like you”.
keyFacts: Refuses to simply moralise: energetic, stylised and darkly funny, yet shows addiction’s squalor
The ideological core is the bookended “Choose Life” monologue
Killer line: “Boyle’s kinetic style and Renton’s ironic voiceover frame heroin as a nihilistic rejection of Thatcherite consumerism — yet the narrative endorses individualism.”
items.examTip: Your spine for narrative-resolution questions: the opening and closing monologues mirror each other.

items.definition: 1980s Edinburgh’s heroin epidemic, unemployment, HIV/AIDS and poverty, far from the tourist city.
items.examples: Tommy, the healthy one, becomes addicted after Allison leaves him, contracts HIV and dies.
keyFacts: Edinburgh had one of the highest HIV infection rates in Europe in the 1980s, linked to shared needles
Unemployment after deindustrialisation left young men with little purpose
The film shows the “other” Scotland behind the tourist image
items.examTip: Use Tommy’s story to show the real cost beneath the cool style.

items.definition: Thatcherism promoted consumerism, individualism and the market over community: “Choose Life” mocks that ideal.
items.examples: Thatcher’s claim “there is no such thing as society” is the ideology Renton finally buys into.
keyFacts: Industrial decline hit Scotland hard, fuelling resentment of Westminster
Consumer goods are listed as if they were life choices
The ending’s theft = Thatcherite self-interest over loyalty
items.examTip: Name the ideology precisely: “Thatcherite neoliberal individualism”.

items.definition: Adapted from Irvine Welsh’s novel; funded by Channel 4 Films on about £1.5 million; a Cool Britannia landmark.
items.examples: Its soundtrack (Iggy Pop, Underworld, Blur, Pulp) and poster style became part of 1990s Britpop culture.
keyFacts: Made by the team behind Shallow Grave (1994): Boyle, producer Andrew Macdonald, writer John Hodge
PolyGram distribution helped it become a global hit
Showed low-budget British film could be commercial and stylish
items.examTip: Institutional context explains its freedom to be provocative.

items.definition: Bold saturated colour, low and wide angles and surreal subjective shots stylise grimy realism into something kinetic.
items.examples: Renton sinking into the red carpet during his overdose, shot from a low angle.
keyFacts: Wide-angle lenses distort the flats, making them claustrophobic
Colour-coded rooms (Swanney’s bright painted den) make squalor striking
Rejects the drab look of traditional British social realism
items.examTip: Contrast its stylised realism with Shaun’s deliberately drab suburbia.

items.definition: Fast cutting, freeze-frames and montage synced to music give the film the energy of a music video.
items.examples: Freeze-frames with on-screen names introduce each character in the opening football match and chase.
keyFacts: Editor Masahiro Hirakubo cuts to the beat of the soundtrack
Freeze-frames suggest Renton controlling his own story
Rhythm makes the high exciting before the crash
items.examTip: Editing as a NARRATIVE tool: freeze-frames show who is telling the story.

items.definition: Renton’s ironic first-person voiceover and a landmark soundtrack shape tone and meaning.
items.examples: “Lust for Life” over the opening chase; “Perfect Day” over the overdose; “Born Slippy” over the ending.
keyFacts: Voiceover = charismatic but unreliable narration
Songs often contrapuntal: “Perfect Day” over near-death
The soundtrack sold the film to a youth audience
items.examTip: Contrapuntal sound is a precise term: use it with “Perfect Day”.

items.definition: Squalid flats and the “worst toilet in Scotland” against consumer goods; McGregor’s charm and Carlyle’s menace.
items.examples: Robert Carlyle’s Begbie glasses a woman in a pub without a second thought.
keyFacts: Ewan McGregor lost weight for the role: the body tells the addiction story
Ewen Bremner’s hapless Spud gives comic warmth
Kelly Macdonald’s Diane, a schoolgirl, undercuts Renton’s cool
items.examTip: Begbie is your evidence for toxic masculinity.

items.definition: Renton and Spud sprint from store security as Renton’s voiceover lists consumer choices he rejects for heroin.
items.examples: Cut to “Lust for Life”; freeze-frames introduce the gang.
keyFacts: Ideology: a direct attack on consumer conformity
Narrative: sets up the unreliable narrator and the circular structure
Form seduces us into the addicts’ worldview before showing its cost
items.examTip: Pair with the ending for any narrative-resolution question.

items.definition: Renton dives into a filthy toilet for his opium suppositories and swims into a clear blue underwater world.
items.examples: Squalor becomes dreamlike: the camera follows him down into calm water and music.
keyFacts: Surreal, subjective sequence as a narrative device
Shows how addiction reframes degradation as escape
Boyle’s signature mix of the grotesque and the beautiful
items.examTip: Evidence of “stylisation” rather than social realism.

items.definition: Allison’s baby dies of neglect in the flat; the scene is stark and unstylised.
items.examples: Silence, then Allison’s scream; the gang respond by cooking up more heroin.
keyFacts: The film’s moral counterweight to its cool style
Shows the real cost of addiction on the innocent
Later the baby hallucination returns crawling on the ceiling during withdrawal
items.examTip: Use to evaluate: the film does not simply glamorise drugs.

items.definition: Renton overdoses and sinks into a red, grave-like carpet, then is dumped outside a hospital.
items.examples: Low-angle shot from inside the hole; Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day” plays.
keyFacts: Subjective form makes the high seductive and lethal at once
Contrapuntal music: beauty over near-death
Ties the spectator to Renton’s point of view
items.examTip: One scene that covers cinematography, sound and narrative.

items.definition: In the Highlands, Renton rants that Scots are “colonised by wankers”, puncturing the romantic image of Scotland.
items.examples: Spoken in a wide shot of green hills: the romantic Scotland image punctured.
keyFacts: Anti-romantic national identity
Political frustration at powerlessness under Westminster
Representation of place: rejecting the tourist Highlands
items.examTip: Great for representation of place and national identity.

items.term: The ending: Renton steals the money
items.definition: After a London drug deal, Renton takes the cash while his mates sleep and walks off promising to “choose life”.
items.examples: “Born Slippy” builds; Renton walks towards camera: “I’m going to be just like you.”
keyFacts: Narrative resolution endorses individualism over collective loyalty
He leaves money for Spud only: a small act of conscience
Bookended voiceover closes the circular structure
items.examTip: THE scene for “How useful is an ideological approach to the narrative resolution?”

items.definition: An episodic, loosely linear structure narrated by an unreliable first-person voiceover, bookended by “Choose Life”.
items.examples: Episodes: the Highlands, Tommy’s decline, withdrawal, the London deal.
keyFacts: Circular framing: the opening chase returns later in the film
Subjective sequences (toilet, overdose, withdrawal) as narrative devices
Todorov: the final equilibrium is a new life built on betrayal
items.examTip: Use precise devices: voiceover, framing narrative, flashback, repetition.

items.definition: Key oppositions include heroin vs consumerism, loyalty vs individualism, Scotland vs England.
items.examples: The ending collapses heroin vs “life”: Renton swaps one addiction (drugs) for another (money and goods).
keyFacts: Lévi-Strauss: narratives are built on binary oppositions
Ideology reveals which side the film finally favours
Begbie (violence) vs Spud (gentleness) as masculine extremes
items.examTip: Sample question: “binary oppositions in the narratives of your chosen films”.

items.definition: Begbie embodies toxic, violent masculinity; Renton is evasive and self-serving; Spud is gentle but powerless.
items.examples: Begbie starts a pub brawl over a dropped glass he threw himself.
keyFacts: Van Zoonen / feminist readings: men in crisis without work
Women (Diane, Allison, Gail) are mostly peripheral
Crisis of masculinity links to deindustrialisation
items.examTip: Compare with Shaun’s man-children for a cross-film paragraph.

items.term: Shaun of the Dead: the key idea
items.definition: A “rom-zom-com” and Marxist satire: modern routine already makes us zombies, so the apocalypse barely changes anything.
items.examples: Shaun walks to the shop twice, before and after the outbreak, and notices nothing different.
keyFacts: Comedy on the surface, social critique underneath
Shaun’s arc is from slacker to responsible adult
Killer line: “Wright uses the zombie genre for Marxist critique: consumer capitalism has already zombified Britain.”
items.examTip: Lead ideology answers with the mirrored walks and the ending montage.

items.definition: Men in their late twenties stuck in arrested adolescence, dead-end jobs and routines in early-2000s suburbia.
items.examples: Shaun works in an electronics shop, bossed by teenage staff; Ed plays video games all day.
keyFacts: Consumerism and low expectations define the characters
The pub and the sofa are their whole world
Liz dumps Shaun because he never changes
items.examTip: Social context + masculinity in one paragraph.

items.term: Cultural context: genre hybrid and Romero homage
items.definition: A postmodern blend of horror, comedy and romance that pays loving homage to George A. Romero’s zombie films.
items.examples: Romero’s Dawn of the Dead (1978) satirised consumerism with zombies in a shopping mall.
keyFacts: Grew from Wright and Pegg’s Channel 4 sitcom Spaced
Full of intertextual references for knowing fans
Romero liked it enough to cast Wright and Pegg as zombies in Land of the Dead (2005)
items.examTip: Genre is part of the narrative specialist area: “genre in relation to narrative”.

items.term: Institutional context: Working Title and StudioCanal
items.definition: A modest-budget British film from Working Title, with Universal distribution, that became a global cult hit.
items.examples: Made for roughly £4 million, it took about $30 million worldwide.
keyFacts: Working Title also made Four Weddings and Notting Hill: British films with transatlantic reach
Wright’s editing-led comedy could be done cheaply
Launched the “Three Flavours Cornetto” trilogy
items.examTip: Compare with Trainspotting’s Channel 4 funding.

items.definition: David M. Dunlap shoots a dull, desaturated suburban London; Shaun appears in blank, zombie-like close-ups.
items.examples: Shaun’s first close-up stares vacantly until Liz snaps him out of it.
keyFacts: The grey palette codes everyday life as half-dead
Parodies horror low-key lighting
Bright colour only in the Winchester’s warm interior
items.examTip: Visual evidence that Shaun is a “zombie” before the zombies arrive.

items.definition: Whip-pans, crash zooms, sound stings and rapid match-cut montages make banal tasks comic and meaningful.
items.examples: A fast montage of Shaun washing, dressing and making tea, repeated later as he prepares to fight.
keyFacts: Repetition of montages marks change and sameness
Editing is a NARRATIVE tool, not just style
Comedy timing is created in the edit
items.examTip: “Editing motif and patterned repetition” is spec language: use it.

items.definition: Electronic stings punctuate cuts; diegetic music is synced to violence for comic effect.
items.examples: Queen’s “Don’t Stop Me Now” plays on the Winchester jukebox as they beat the zombie landlord.
keyFacts: Contrapuntal: upbeat songs over slaughter
Sound bridges link scenes and gags
Ironic song choices comment on the action
items.examTip: Pair with Trainspotting’s needle-drops for comparison.

items.definition: The corner shop, the Winchester pub, garden sheds and very English weapons: a cricket bat, a spade, vinyl records.
items.examples: They choose which LPs to throw at zombies, sparing the ones they like.
keyFacts: Simon Pegg’s everyman Shaun; Nick Frost’s man-child Ed
Kate Ashfield’s Liz drives Shaun’s change
Bill Nighy’s Philip: the distant stepfather Shaun reconciles with
items.examTip: British national identity through props and setting.

items.term: The mirrored walk to the shop
items.definition: Shaun’s half-asleep walk to the corner shop is repeated after the outbreak with the same framing and rhythm.
items.examples: Both are long handheld tracking takes along the same route; the second time zombies and blood are everywhere.
keyFacts: Ideology: consumer routine already equals zombiehood
Narrative: repetition as patterning, a parallel structure
Pure form carrying meaning
items.examTip: Your single best ideology evidence for Shaun.

items.definition: In the first pub scene a drunk Ed lists tomorrow’s plans, a coded preview of the zombie plot to come.
items.examples: Ed’s day (a “Bloody Mary” first thing, “a bite” at one pub, a stagger back to the Winchester) comes true in zombie form; Shaun’s own plan (“go to the Winchester, have a nice cold pint, and wait for all this to blow over”) becomes a running gag.
keyFacts: Wright’s parodic, self-aware narrative structure
Rewards active spectators on rewatching
Postmodern playfulness with narrative
items.examTip: Evidence for any narrative structure question.

items.definition: Shaun’s bitten mother turns in the Winchester, and Shaun must shoot her.
items.examples: The comedy stops; close-ups and a quiet score hold on Shaun’s grief.
keyFacts: Shaun’s moment of adult responsibility
Tonal shift shows the film’s emotional core
Completes his arc away from the man-child
items.examTip: Use to show the film is more than parody.

items.term: The Winchester siege: “Don’t Stop Me Now”
items.definition: Shaun, Liz and Ed beat the zombie landlord with pool cues in time to Queen on the jukebox.
items.examples: Choreographed violence synced to the beat; the jukebox flashes.
keyFacts: Diegetic music synced to action: comedy and horror fused
The pub as a last bastion of British identity
Advances Shaun’s turn towards responsibility
items.examTip: Aesthetics + narrative in one scene.

items.definition: Six months on, TV shows zombies used as cheap labour and game-show entertainment; zombie Ed lives in the shed.
items.examples: Channel-flicking montage of news and chat shows; Shaun plays video games with chained Ed.
keyFacts: Marxist punchline: capitalism absorbs the undead as labour and entertainment
Todorov parodied: the new equilibrium looks almost exactly like the old one
Shaun keeps both Liz and Ed: a compromise ending
items.examTip: THE scene for an ideological reading of the narrative resolution.

subtopics.title: Narrative and ideology in Shaun of the Dead

items.definition: A linear, conventional three-act structure, made parodic by foreshadowing, repetition and genre knowingness.
items.examples: Act 1: Liz dumps Shaun. Act 2: the outbreak and the journey. Act 3: the Winchester siege.
keyFacts: Todorov: equilibrium, disruption, recognition, repair, new equilibrium
Propp: Shaun as hero, Liz as princess figure, Philip as false father
Genre conventions are followed in order to be mocked
items.examTip: Contrast with Trainspotting’s episodic, unreliable structure.

items.definition: Alive vs undead, responsibility vs slacking, pub vs home; Marxist ideology reveals the living/dead line is fake.
items.examples: Shaun and the zombies move the same way in the mirrored walks.
keyFacts: The film blurs its own oppositions to make its point
Liz vs Ed: adulthood vs adolescence
Resolved by compromise, not victory
items.examTip: Ideology lets you say WHY the oppositions blur.

items.definition: Hegemonic masculinity is inverted: the men are man-children; Shaun’s arc is towards care, not toughness.
items.examples: Shaun finally takes charge, makes plans and protects Liz and his mum.
keyFacts: A modern, failing masculinity
Ed represents permanent adolescence
Philip’s stiff, traditional fatherhood is reconciled before he dies
items.examTip: Cross-film comparison with Trainspotting’s Begbie and Renton.

items.definition: Story (fabula) is events in time order; plot (syuzhet) is how the film arranges and shows them.
items.examples: Trainspotting’s plot shuffles and frames events; Shaun’s plot follows story order.
keyFacts: From Russian Formalism, developed by Bordwell
Ellipsis and duration: what is cut out and how long things last
Spec: “the formalist conception of narrative based on the distinction between story and plot”
items.examTip: Use the terms story/plot to show precise narrative knowledge.

items.definition: Narratives move from equilibrium to disruption, recognition, repair and a new equilibrium.
items.examples: Shaun’s new equilibrium is almost the old one; Renton’s is built on betrayal.
keyFacts: Useful for judging narrative resolution
Endings carry ideology: what kind of order is restored?
Limit: not every film resolves neatly
items.examTip: Always ask what the NEW equilibrium says ideologically.

items.definition: Structuralism: meaning comes from opposed pairs that the narrative explores and resolves.
items.examples: Life vs death, loyalty vs self-interest, conformity vs rebellion.
keyFacts: Spec: “the structuralist conception of narrative based on binary oppositions”
Ideology decides which side the film privileges
Oppositions also exist in form: colour, lighting, sound
items.examTip: Sample stem uses binary oppositions: have two per film ready.

items.definition: Propp found folk tales use the same roles: hero, villain, donor, helper, princess, dispatcher, false hero.
items.examples: Shaun as hero; Ed as hapless helper; the faun in Pan’s Labyrinth as donor/dispatcher.
keyFacts: From Morphology of the Folktale (1928)
Works best on genre narratives
Can be ideological: who gets to be the hero?
items.examTip: Use briefly; do not let it replace film-form analysis.

items.definition: Voiceover, flashback, framing narrative, open endings, repetition and foreshadowing shape how a story is told.
items.examples: Renton’s voiceover; Shaun’s foreshadowed plan; City of God’s flashbacks.
keyFacts: Restricted vs omniscient narration controls what the spectator knows
Unreliable narrators create ambiguity
The spec lists these devices directly
items.examTip: Name a device, then show its effect on the spectator.

items.definition: Genre conventions shape narrative expectations; films repeat and vary them (Steve Neale: repetition and difference).
items.examples: Shaun follows zombie-film structure to parody it; Trainspotting borrows the crime-caper ending.
keyFacts: Rick Altman: semantic (iconography) and syntactic (structure) elements of genre
Hybrid genres (rom-zom-com) mix conventions
Genre is part of the narrative specialist area for British film
items.examTip: Use genre to explain WHY a narrative is shaped as it is.

items.definition: Who wins, who is punished and how a story ends express values: narrative structure carries ideology.
items.examples: Renton rewarded for betrayal; zombies absorbed into capitalism.
keyFacts: Spec: “how narrative can function as an ideological framework”
Endings are the clearest site of ideology
Evaluate: endings can also be ironic or ambiguous
items.examTip: This item links both specialist areas: use it in every Section C essay.
